comments.author: zone411
comments.text: For context, OpenAI's 4 new papers resolve 8 problems of the Top 500 Open Problems in Math list (LLM ranked, https://proofatlas.ai/open-problems/ ). They include: #25 — Matrix-multiplication exponent equals two. The paper gives the exact exponent 9/4 over every field, refuting the conjecture. #89 — Strongly polynomial linear programming (Smale’s ninth problem). The same paper also gives polynomial-time algorithms for #64 — Mean-payoff games, #65 — Parity games, #340 — Condon’s simple stochastic games. #183 — Polynomial diameter bound for polytopes, #130 — Polynomial pivot rule for the simplex method, both refuted. Some pairs of vertices are superpolynomially far apart. #137 — Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture. For every fixed number of petals r, the paper proves the conjectured Cᵣᵏ bound. (rankings post Riemann (#2) and VP vs VNP (#31)).

comments.author: StableAlkyne
comments.text: We've seen so much interesting work come out of OpenAI and Anthropic in the last few weeks. It really feels like both have tapped into the pioneering spirit of the old Bell Labs. But, Bell Labs existed as part of an agreement with the government that AT&T's monopoly would be used for the public good. OpenAI and Anthropic don't really have much use for this beyond PR... If even the prestige from Riemann's Hypothesis couldn't boost ANT, what is the reason for them devoting such a huge fraction of their R&D budget to unrelated (though impactful) problems? Scaring mathematicians into burning their non-existent research budgets on tokens in order to make a couple million dollars? Open weight models are to the point that most business cases are completely solved by them, at a fraction of the price of Claude, Copilot, or OpenAI. Unfortunately, the average business doesn't care that the AI can solve frontier problems: they just need something to summarize emails or give an executive a summary of the day's headlines. The market is just waiting for a cheap provider that is just as turnkey... Which isn't exactly a high barrier these days. IMO there is space for a unicorn to emerge in the next few years to eat everyone's lunch.

comments.author: hunter2_
comments.text: This is really cool. I have a suggestion, though: the samples within a button seem to have several modification types including a pitch shifter. For example, "DOWN4" under the "Multi-sampled sounds" heading sounds nearly a semitone lower than the other DOWN variants. I suggest eliminating all pitch shifting (or at least confining your use to a few cents), leaving only timbre variation. Go nuts creating variation through EQ, distortion, formant shifting, reflections/delay/reverb, etc. but keep the pitch locked. Why? Because the pitch of everything in this world is based on its resonant frequency, which is based on the size of whatever can vibrate, and in the case of a button it's resonating based on the size of the button. Many aspects of the sound would change based on things like how quickly the button is pushed or how much dampening the finger pushing it imparts, but the fundamental pitch is not one of them. When playing a violin, if you move up the fingerboard, the pitch of the string increases. But if instead of playing the string you knock on the body as if knocking on someone's front door, the main pitch of that knocking never changes. The sympathetic vibrations of the strings will have frequencies that vary as the finger position varies, and the brightness and RT60 of the reverberation through the wood will vary from knock to knock, but the fundamental frequency generally excited by the knock only changes if the violin's volumetric size changes, and it never will. Maybe a drum is a better example than a violin, since it's "unpitched" and yet still gets tuned to have some fundamental frequency. Only the noisy stuff varies from hit to hit, and the fundamental frequency does not (until you re-tune, or from temperature/humidity changing).

comments.author: amluto
comments.text: This shared LV cache thing is, in my mind, ridiculous. Web browser developers learned, quite a while ago, that caches need to be separated for different origins. Inference servers should add a similar feature: allow API calls to specify cache separation keys that prevent one security context from probing another context’s cache. As for the step size issue, Google recently had a post about producing exactly consistent output across different kernels (specifically by defining a deterministic prefill algorithm and then requiring all kernels to generate results exactly equal to prefilling on the sequence in question). More broadly, I think it’s a bit odd to frame this as “models” communicating. This is software communicating, and the models happen to be running the software.

comments.author: tsimionescu
comments.text: None of the attacks discussed here are realistic in any way. They require a bunch of extremely improbable conditions to hold, and a huge amount of information on the exact details of the hardware and software stack. - the two agents must be aware of each other and must have pre-shared messages to check - they can't spontaneously discover each other and start communicating in this way - they must know the details of the inference server they are running under and its possible kernels and its limits (what is a "short prompt" vs "a long prompt" for this setup) - they must have a way to run at almost the same time - the prefix cache must have little contention so that their blocks can't be evicted (note: the article mostly talks about KV cache, but it's actually the prefix cache that is relevant here) - the models need either (1) direct access to the numerical results of the inference process, instead of the text that vLLM provides, (2) access to the exact responses that a helper model will produce with the short-kernel numerical results vs the long-kernel numerical results; this is the most critical step that is impossible to reproduce on any common kind of deployment - there must not be any other kind of variability in the system (different GPUs, multiple inference servers behind a load balancer, more complex distributed inference setups) The post also mentions all of these limitations, and that the scheme entirely collapses if any of them don't hold. It's a cool idea, but it's a purely theoretical thing that has 0 real-world implications.

comments.author: devy
comments.text: Frontier models today can easily figure this out. The less frontier models as of right now are probably going to take a long horizon session to figure out this type of "side channel" comms. However, posting this in depth step by step on the internet and discussed in open forums like here, now all models definitely know about this trick now.

comments.author: kgeist
comments.text: If a single vLLM instance handles both prefill and decode without disaggregation, I can think of another way. Alice reads a long document every N seconds to transmit a 1, and does nothing to transmit a 0. Bob, in its own loop, measures the time using bash, generates some random text and writes it to a file, and then checks the time again to estimate its own tokens per second (file length / elapsed time). The trick is that when a vLLM instance handles both prefill and decode, decoding slows down measurably because vLLM has to alternate between prefill and decode phases. It assumes only 2 agents are running, though, but it doesn't require fine-tuning or a second helper model.

comments.author: mananaysiempre
comments.text: A couple of notes: - There’s also the notation 0 for the empty (never, noreturn) type. In addition to matching the number of members, the notations 0 and 1 make sense also as units (neutral elements) of addition and multiplication respectively: 0 + A ≅ A + 0 ≅ A, 1 × A ≅ A × 1 ≅ A in a natural way[1]; and also 0 × A ≅ A × 0 ≅ 0. - That a constant dependent sum is a product, and a constant dependent product is an exponential, is (undeniably confusing at first but) just[2] the naïve schoolbook definition that A × B = B added to itself A times and A^B = A multiplied by itself B times. - That a constant dependent product is a function type is just the naïve definition that a function is a table of its values at each input (a tuple, with elements numbered by the possible inputs). A dependent function ( = dependent product), then, is the same thing but the allowable values in each cell of the table vary depending on the cell. - That the function type is the exponential type is also part of common set-theory notation. For instance, 2^ℕ is a not-infrequent name for the set in the Cantor theorem (subsets of the naturals). [1] As in, those are not literally the same type but are one-to-one in a single natural way. The word “natural” here has a surprisingly deep technical meaning but one that corresponds to the colloquial pretty well. [2] “Just”, “simply”, etc. are as usual terms of art that mean that the statement feels very simple once you get it , and conversely that if it does not feel simple then you haven’t gotten it and should stop and think until it does. That thinking can take substantial time and effort.

comments.author: elhospitaler
comments.text: I did my PhD at the Baker lab, haven't had the time to properly read this over but some initial thoughts: Makes total sense that they'd be working on this, it's something we discussed in the lab as well as the likely future of this work - true integration of the language modeling capabilities with proteins, natively multimodal like it's done with images. Five years ago we laughed at people with galaxy brained ideas to train / fuse a protein and natural language model, advertising this idea of "give me a natural language request and the model spits out the sequence that does the thing". There are many objections - the annotated data is not there, trying to pose everything as a language modeling objective sounded really naive at the time, and there are lots of tasks that are structural/chemical in nature that require inference based on physical and chemical principles, which interpolating machine learning models shouldn't be able to do. Most of these objections still exist, but now we aren't laughing. I do think eventually these models will get there. That said, this work of course advertises far more than it accomplishes/has some things that have me holding judgement. One is I don't see how they did train-test splitting, or if they attempted this at all. This is really important - for some of these tasks, they are comparing against "specialized models" that did pretty rigorous holdout evaluation. Also binder design is basically the easiest task, super solved a million times in the past few years, and their designs just made helical bundles, I don't think this is particularly impressive in terms of pushing the frontier. There is a hierarchy of difficult problems in protein design and this is just really easy, especially because experimentally these helical bundles bind really well and make strong interfaces. The antibody CDR design tasks are also probably fairly trivial? I'm not sure, I'm not deep into antibody dev/design but there are lots of structures and sequences of anti-pdl-1 antibodies, so again a case of train-test split. I'd be curious to see sequence homology to these published antibodies. But yeah, my take is that at the object level, this work is not super impressive. At one level of remove, the fact that they are getting an LLM to do these tasks that are normally done by specialized protein language or structure models is impressive. And then at one more level of remove, it's a big gauntlet thrown, proof that they are pursuing this line of research. I wouldn't be surprised if it works much better, soon, with the pace of these things. And we know Anthropic is working on this as well - https://xinmingtu.cn/blog/2026/claude-opus-5-5-protein-seque... . Might have to find a new line of work soon lol, thought I had at least another 5 years left.

comments.author: plaidfuji
comments.text: This is interesting, although the “beyond specialized models” feels a bit premature. It seems like GPT can act like a glue layer between the highly specialized models that carry out each specific sub-task in a protein design workflow… and in some cases, can outperform specialized models at those tasks. I’ve noticed that LLMs are very good at this type of glue work between highly specialized fields. It used to be quite difficult to “connect” your own work to adjacent tools made by other SMEs, sometimes so difficult that it was impractical. I suspect one of the biggest impacts of LLMs on science will be the enablement of more frictionless collaboration and higher-level integration of specialized capabilities in a single study. That said, the use of “intrinsic design capabilities” in the title of this article is misleading, as much of the demonstrated capabilities involve tool calls, and/or need outside support by the same specialized models they claim to have moved beyond in order to arrive at useful results.

comments.author: FinnLobsien
comments.text: Reality isn't deterministic. Everyone rationally understands this, but most people don't act on it. It's foolish to believe that the quality of one's results scales linearly with planning, strategizing, and so on. We've all made intricate plans that went nowhere and done off-the-cuff things that became breakthroughs. I think the important mental model here is expected value: What's the potential upside and downside and what probability do I assign to those outcomes? For everything you do, you should be able to make a credible case that it could lead to a great outcome, but don't bet everything on one scenario. This creates the mental space to not pick favorites among approaches and act on real results (vs. insisting on the solution that was so elegant in your head). "Flailing" (I'd call it tinkering) falls apart in two scenarios: -When one attempt's failure doesn't take you back where you started, but makes you significantly worse off (e.g. larges-scale production infrastructure) -When the feedback loop isn't based on the results you're trying to achieve (e.g. users like your feature, but an exec doesn't, so the exec deprecates it)

comments.author: nickcw
comments.text: The main boxed formula is equivalent to this Machin style formula for pi pi = 4 arctan 4/7 + 4 arctan 1/8 + 2 arctan 8/31 + 2 arctan 1/32 Because each of the denominators in the arctans is a power or 2 or 1 different from a power of 2, we can make a BBP formula from it to calculate any hex digit of pi without calculating the previous ones. I wrote a reasonably accessible account of how this works in https://scholarlycommons.pacific.edu/euleriana/vol3/iss1/3/ (which is referenced in the article!) The boxed formula is exciting because it has been rearranged so that it has a single common denominator, so only needs 1 division per term. It is the divisions which are slow so reducing the number of them speeds up the calculation. That plus another trick makes the calculation run 40% faster than the best known BBP formula. > There’s a choice hiding in the last step of Bellard’s terse derivation. That made me laugh. It took me several days to figure out Bellard's terse derivation :-)

comments.author: Tiberium
comments.text: For the general picture: the Xbox version of the game was leaked by Cyberleek - first the resources, then the game binary. Because modern Xbox is very close to a Windows PC with some extra Xbox stuff, running the actual game code isn't hard, it's mostly about compatibility and graphics, plus the binary doesn't have any special DRM/obfuscation. The current projects (xcl and VIctory) basically take a Wine-like approach. The main problems they have to solve, as I understand: - The game ships with raw RDNA 2 shaders, so the projects have to translate that to another format, e.g. DXIL for DirectX 12, and compile those shaders. So you need a good translation/recompilation pipeline, if it's bad, the shaders will be bloated and perform poorly - Xbox has unified memory, while most PCs do not, so you have to add a lot of workarounds and book-keeping for the game to work properly with that - Xbox's DirectX 12 differs from the normal Windows one in some ways, and the game uses Xbox-specific texture formats with DirectStorage I just wanted to share this because there's a lot of misconceptions going around about this being a "recomp" or something like that. Decompiling the entire binary (it's about 100MB of real executable machine code) will be a much bigger effort than getting this binary to run.
